title: Structured fallback grammar and SDK adaptor — PRD sketch
body:
Summary:

This PRD sketch proposes a compact, machine-readable fallback grammar for hosted API streaming responses plus a lightweight SDK adaptor pattern that makes client fallback/resume, tool-handshake, and structured-output reconciliation predictable and easy for developers to adopt. The goal is to reduce application-level complexity when the server returns partial, downgraded, or hybrid (text + tool) results while preserving low latency and clear observability.

Problem statement:

Teams building on the Hosted API need dependable behavior when streaming responses are interrupted, downgraded to simpler outputs, or when tool-calls are proxied/fallbacked. Current client implementations re-implement ad-hoc heuristics: partial JSON repairs, brittle regex extraction, or complicated replay logic. This leads to developer friction, poor UX on flaky networks, and production bugs during rollouts of new tool integrations or compact fallback models.

Principles and constraints:

- Keep wire protocol minimal: small tokens/markers rather than a heavy schema for every message.
- Machine-first grammar: fallback signals must be parseable without heuristics.
- SDK ergonomics: provide a single compact adaptor that handles fallback grammar, resume, and typed binding to tool outputs.
- Backwards compatible with existing incremental/partial-response streams.
- Instrumentation-friendly: every fallback/resume should emit structured telemetry.

Goals (what success looks like):

- A defined fallback grammar that covers: model-degraded outputs, truncated/partial JSON, tool-handshake fallthrough, and explicit resume checkpoints.
- An SDK adaptor for JS + Python that: normalizes events, exposes typed tool results, provides resume helpers, and emits compact telemetry events developers can wire to Console tracing.
- Developer docs and 6 internal sample apps demonstrating edge cases (mobile with intermittent networks, server-driven fallback to a cheaper model, tool proxy failure).
- Measurable reduction in customer bug reports for partial streams and structured output breakages (target: 60% reduction quarter-over-quarter for onboarding customers).

Non-goals:

- Full redesign of streaming frame protocol (we extend, not replace).
- Supporting all legacy SDKs in first wave — ship JS + Python first.

User scenarios (concrete examples):

1) Mobile chat: intermittent network causes short disconnect during a long answer. The client should be able to resume streaming from last checkpoint and mark sections generated after the disconnect as "speculative" until confirmed.

2) Tool-backed workflow: model initiates a tool call, the tool times out at the provider side. Server falls back to a summary-only path. Client receives a compact fallback frame that clearly indicates the tool result is missing and provides "best-effort-summary" as a field. The app decides whether to surface a degraded action to the user or queue a retry.

3) Schema-first integration: product team expects a typed JSON payload for downstream ingestion. If the model returns partial JSON (truncated or with extra fields), the SDK should present a reconciliation result: parsed fields, parse-errors, and recommended fallback hooks.

Design: fallback grammar (high level)

We introduce a minimal set of streaming frame markers embedded in the existing stream that are intentionally compact and token-oriented. The grammar is primarily for machine consumption and optional for simple clients. Example markers (human-readable representation):

- FRAME:CHECKPOINT:id=uuid;offset=123;model=mosaic-lite
  -> server checkpoint indicating a durable resume point and KV offset for streaming sequence.

- FRAME:FALLBACK:reason=tool-timeout;tag=best-effort-summary;fallback-model=ultra-small
  -> server explicitly signals that a fallback strategy was used for the immediately preceding content. Contains a short taxonomy reason and optional fallback model id.

- FRAME:STRUCTURE:begin:schema_id=v1.2;req=[title,items];approx_size=small
  -> marks the start of a structured delivery (will be followed by chunked JSON-literals or typed frames).

- FRAME:STRUCTURE:partial:cursor=45;error=truncated
  -> indicates partial structured payload with an annotated error code.

- FRAME:RESUME:token=base64;hint=prefer-priority
  -> client/server resume token exchange for rejoining a session. Token is opaque to client but passed back to API.

These markers are small ASCII prefix lines at the start of a stream chunk (or as discrete events in an evented stream) and are deliberately terse to avoid token inflation. The runtime will map these to JSON events before SDK consumption.

Structured output reconciliation semantics:

The SDK adaptor must expose a reconciliation object for each STRUCTURE block with fields: parsed_fields (map), parse_errors (list), completeness_percentage (string), original_tokens (string snippet), fallback_reason (optional). The heuristic rules for reconciliation are: attempt JSON-LD style merging for partial chunks, prefer last-wins for conflicting fields in streaming order, and annotate any field whose type/shape deviates from schema with a parse_error entry.

Tool-handshake and fallback rules:

- Tool-call starts with a typed REQUEST frame with expected schema for tool input.
- The tool provider may return TOOL:OK, TOOL:ERROR, TOOL:TIMEOUT frames. On TOOL:ERROR/TIMEOUT the server may emit FALLBACK with a recommended fallback_tag.
- Clients using our SDK adaptor will receive a single coherent ToolResult object with: status (ok/error/timeout), raw_output (string), typed_output (parsed if available), fallback_suggestion (enum: retry, summary, omit).

SDK adaptor ergonomics (JS + Python core ideas):

1) Single entrypoint: createAdapter(stream, options) returns:
   - on('structured', handler(recon))
   - on('checkpoint', handler(info))
   - on('fallback', handler(info))
   - resume(resume_token) -> returns a small async helper that posts resume and streams the rest.

2) Backpressure-friendly callbacks: allow callback handlers to return "PAUSE/CONTINUE" signals (promises or futures) so the application can apply client-side buffering without losing order.

3) Pluggable parsers: expose parser hooks for typed schemas so teams can register fast, schema-compiled parsers for STRUCTURE blocks.

4) Conservative defaults: if a developer does not opt-in to typed parsing, the adaptor provides a safe, validated JSON blob plus parse_errors and a completeness score; apps can still render human-friendly fallback_text.

Observability and telemetry requirements:

Minimal telemetry events emitted by adaptor per session (compact, customer-PII-free):
- fallback_emitted {reason, fallback_model, elapsed_ms}
- resume_attempt {success:boolean, latency_ms, resume_token_present}
- structure_parse {schema_id, completeness_pct, parse_errors_count}
- tool_call_outcome {tool, status, error_code}
Telemetry is emitted to Console tracing with counters and optional sampling. Each event includes a trace_id/session_id mapping to the Redwood Console for debugging.

Backward compatibility and migration plan:

- Phase 0 (internal testing): server emits markers wrapped as secondary lines in event streams; internal SDKs parse and verify behavior on test sandboxes.
- Phase 1 (opt-in beta): public Hosted API accepts param streaming_fallback=grammar-v1 and docs show how to opt-in. Ship JS and Python adapters.
- Phase 2 (gradual default): enable grammar for new customers by default, keep old behavior for existing tenants for 90 days with a sunset notice.

Rollout safety and toggles:

- Feature flag per-tenant: streaming_fallback: off | grammar-v1 | grammar-v1-preview.
- Fallback telemetry sampling switch for high-volume tenants.

Success metrics and targets:

- Developer adoption: 30% of new Hosted API integrations activate grammar-v1 within 3 months of GA.
- Errors: reduce structured-output parse incidents reported by customer SREs by 60% for tenants using the adaptor.
- Latency: average end-to-end additional tokens/bytes due to markers <1% of typical response size.

Risks and mitigations:

- Token inflation: markers add bytes — keep markers terse and optional; provide binary-encoded markers for high-volume flows in a later iteration.
- SDK complexity: risk of heavy SDK surface — ship minimal adaptor with pluggable optional features and clear defaults.
- Schema churn: schemas evolve — support schema_id versioning and a server-provided compatibility header.

Open questions for engineering:

- Should resume tokens be entirely opaque or carry a small HMAC verifiable by clients for cheaper client-side checks?
- What is the best compact encoding for markers on binary streams (CRLF-delimited ASCII vs. TLV-style)?

Next steps and owners:

- Product: finalize grammar tokens and taxonomy (owner: Priya Nair) — due 2025-03-10.
- Serving runtime: prototype server marker emission and resume handshake (owner: Elliot Kim) — spike 2 weeks.
- SDK: implement JS adaptor alpha with unit tests and telemetry hooks (owner: Ava Chen) — initial alpha 2025-03-24.
- Docs: developer guide and migration checklist (owner: Diego Martinez) — draft 2025-04-07.

Appendix: compact example (simulated stream)

[FRAME:CHECKPOINT:id=3f4a;offset=512;model=fast-lite]
Hello, here is the first part of the answer.
[FRAME:STRUCTURE:begin:schema_id=product-list;req=[id,name,price]]
{"items":[{"id":1,"name":"widget","price":9}
[FRAME:STRUCTURE:partial:cursor=1;error=truncated]
[FRAME:FALLBACK:reason=tool-timeout;tag=summary;fallback-model=ultra-small]
{"summary":"Tool timed out — best effort summary: contains 12 items"}
[FRAME:RESUME:token=Z3Vlc3Q=;hint=prefer-priority]

This sketch intentionally favors pragmatic choices that reduce developer lift for common failure modes while keeping the stream efficient for production traffic. Feedback welcome — add comments or ping me in #product-hosted-api.
